item.title: Amatlas: A 2D Array Architecture for Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Fits surface code up to distance d=25 on single VCU129 FPGA, achieving average decoding time of 462 ns per round at physical error rate p=0.1% and threshold of 0.72% under circuit-level noise.

Grade 0.514 · 3.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Seita Tsuboi, Hidetsugu Irie, Junichiro Kadomoto

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate for code distances d=5 to 21 showing a threshold of 0.72%, scaling of logical error rate with growth period K, and violin plots of decoding time distribution per round up to d=25.

Asks

Can Union-Find surface-code decoding scale to large code distances on planar hardware without a central controller enforcing array-wide stage synchronization?

Before

Helios reached d=17 at 23.7 ns per round under circuit-level noise on same FPGA; Collision Clustering reached d=23 at 1.18 µs per round; LCD reached d=17 at 460 ns per round on VU19P.

But

Circuit-level depolarizing noise model on rotated surface code; hook edges decomposed into two-edge paths; 99.99th percentile decoding time exceeds 1 µs for d≥17.

Tools

2D array of processing elements · local PE memory for temporal rounds · token-based Union-Find decoding · RTL FPGA implementation on AMD Xilinx VCU129 (VU29P)

Abstract

Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.

item.title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Code distance d≥21 achieves logical error rates below 10−10 per syndrome cycle. Architecture integrates over 120,000 logical qubits on 100 mm × 100 mm chip using CMOS-compatible multiplexing.

Grade 0.505 · 3.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Masahiro Tadokoro, Tetsuo Kodera

Asks

How to design a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture that integrates error correction, spin shuttling, wiring constraints, and transversal logical gates.

But

Numerical and analytical architecture model based on currently demonstrated physical silicon spin qubit parameters; assumes optimized CMOS multiplexing efficiency.

Tools

rotated surface code · 1D spin shuttling lanes · cross junctions for routing and transversal CNOT · CMOS-compatible multiplexed wiring model

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below 10⁻¹⁰ per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm × 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.

item.title: Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — CNN decoders trained via a 1000-fold faster Pauli-frame loss sampler achieve a 2×103-fold reduction in logical error rate per logical qubit per round on the [[144,12,12]] Gross code at p=1% under pure loss compared to pure Pauli noise.

Grade 0.496 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · J. Wilson Staples, Winston Fu, Yihe Dong, Jeff D. Thompson

Figure

Logical error rate per round per logical qubit p~L versus physical error rate p for the walking Gross code across loss fractions λ∈[0,1], contrasting CNN decoding with the baseline Uniform Mixture decoder.

Asks

Can high-rate qLDPC codes be simulated and decoded effectively under qubit loss with delayed heralding and skipped gates?

Before

Uniform Mixture decoder (Relay-BP on an averaged matching hypergraph) had ≈103 higher logical error rate at p=0.7% and loss fraction λ=0.98; most-likely error decoding failed to certify within 900 s.

But

Applies strictly to circuits satisfying the zero-reference condition (noiseless all-zeros measurement valid despite skipped entangling gates). Assumes three-outcome loss measurements and static non-interacting lost states |L⟩.

Tools

slim Pauli-frame loss sampler · Tanner-graph CNN decoder · walking Gross code circuit · stim framework

Abstract

Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, textttslim, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. For the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle (Gross) code, we study a walking syndrome extraction circuit with Pauli and loss errors. For physical error rates p<1%, we observe a more than 10³-fold lower logical error rate for a pure loss model, relative to a pure Pauli error model at the same physical error rate, along with significantly enhanced sub-threshold error rate scaling. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.

item.title: Constructively Embedding Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Decomposing quantum LDPC Tanner graph hardware layout into continuous embedding, Hungarian grid assignment, and shortest-path routing constructs routed code geometries and benchmarks them across footprint, communication overhead, and congestion.

Grade 0.491 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Yucheng He, Todd A. Brun

Figure

Total layout cost versus scale parameter s for the radius-2 HaPPY code under rectilinear and octilinear 2D and 3D geometries, comparing the default pipeline against single-stage and full ablations.

Asks

How can quantum error-correcting codes with nonlocal Tanner graphs be systematically and constructively mapped onto physical hardware routing lattices?

But

Heuristic three-stage pipeline rather than globally optimal layout; proxy metrics evaluate geometric costs rather than physical circuit-level or noise-threshold simulations.

Tools

spectral embedding · multidimensional scaling (MDS) · Fruchterman–Reingold spring layout · Hungarian algorithm (linear assignment) · canonical shortest-path and congestion-aware A* routing

Abstract

Implementing quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) requires more than favorable algebraic parameters: the interactions among data qubits and ancillas must also fit physical hardware. Surface codes map naturally onto two-dimensional arrays, but many quantum LDPC codes have Tanner graphs with nonlocal connections. We develop a constructive pipeline that maps a QECC's Tanner graph to the targeted hardware lattice in three stages (continuous embedding, grid assignment, and path routing). Continuous embeddings reveal the geometric structure of the code, including differences between stabilizer generator sets of the same code. The discrete stages produce explicit routed layouts that we can characterize and compare using proxy metrics for footprint, communication overhead, and congestion for syndrome extraction. We examine three continuous embedding methods: multidimensional scaling (distance-based), spectral embedding (Laplacian-based), and spring layout (force-based) for the first stage. Experiments across tested codes show how routing geometry, dimension, and scale selection affect the resulting costs. In ablation studies on the radius-2 (R2) HaPPY code, graph-aware methods for continuous embedding and the choice of path-routing algorithm matter more than the grid assignment under our chosen weights in the cost function. Changing the continuous embedding reveals a trade-off: MDS incurs greater communication overhead than spectral embedding over most tested scales, while spring layout can reduce communication overhead at intermediate scales but increases congestion and is less stable across scales.

item.title: High-Throughput GPU Decoding of Quantum Bivariate Bicycle Codes under Circuit-Level Noise
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Sustains 1 μs syndrome arrival interval across bivariate bicycle codes up to [[144,12,12]] on an RTX 5090 with median commit delays of 63–144 μs. Provides 120× higher throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding and reaches 7.58×10−6 logical failures per round at p=0.002.

Grade 0.476 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Aditya Sodhani, Keshab K. Parhi

Figure

Architecture diagram of the GPU execution pipeline, showing persistent worker thread blocks that independently process overlapping A windows and resolve B gaps directly in shared memory without host round trips.

Asks

Can GPU decoders for bivariate bicycle codes under circuit-level noise achieve the 1 μs real-time streaming throughput needed by superconducting quantum error correction?

Before

Sequential sliding-window BP-SF on an RTX 5060 Ti sustained arrivals of 2.97 ms per round, with pL=11.9×10−6 per round at p=0.002 (published BP-SF).

But

Circuit-level noise simulations with independent Z-basis streams without joint X/Z correlation tracking; emulates round arrivals via an on-chip clock rather than live host-to-device streaming.

Tools

Parallel-window decoding · Min-sum belief propagation with Relay-BP recovery · Compressed shared-memory Tanner graph state · Persistent GPU thread blocks · NVIDIA RTX 5090

Abstract

Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 μs across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 μs median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides 120× higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at p=0.002, our proposed decoder achieves 7.58×10⁻⁶ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.

item.title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Survey of qudit quantum information hardware demonstrates that multi-level d>2 architectures match the Hilbert space of 70 qubits using 24 qudits with d=8, achieving gate-depth reductions exceeding one order of magnitude in dedicated quantum simulations.

Grade 0.442 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik

Figure

Landscape of qudit implementations showing controllable qudit dimension d on the horizontal axis versus the number of interacting qudits n on the vertical axis across experimental platforms.

Asks

What is the current experimental state of the art in high-fidelity state preparation, control, measurement, and fault tolerance across diverse qudit platforms?

But

Increased spectral crowding, heightened sensitivity to phase decoherence, energy relaxation across higher levels, and elevated classical and quantum crosstalk.

Tools

trapped ions · superconducting circuits · solid-state nuclear spins · photonic circuits · neutral atoms

Abstract

Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

item.title: Using a static spacetime subsystem code to calculate Floquet code distance
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Mapping a Floquet code on n physical qubits with period Pˆ and k logical qubits across T=(n+1)Pˆd0 (or +1) time steps yields an $[[nT, k, d]]$ static spacetime subsystem code whose distance equals the spacetime distance of the Floquet code.

Grade 0.423 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Ethan Egger, Milad Marvian

Asks

Can Floquet code distance be calculated directly by mapping the dynamical measurement sequence to a static spacetime subsystem code that preserves code distance?

Before

Standard spacetime code mappings produced subsystem codes whose distance only provided an upper bound on circuit fault distance, because boundary stabilizers had no corresponding detectors.

But

Serial measurements; Clifford circuits with Pauli measurements; applies to the steady state of periodic measurement sequences after reaching maximum instantaneous stabilizer group size.

Tools

spacetime subsystem codes · Floquet codes · periodic time-like gauge boundary conditions · detector-to-stabilizer mapping

Abstract

Dynamical codes, including Floquet codes, can capture time-dependent phenomena in quantum error correction circuits that are absent from static stabilizer or subsystem codes, such as detecting regions and error propagation. They are also capable of preserving more logical qubits than corresponding schemes in which the same syndrome-extraction measurements are performed without being distributed over time. However, evaluating the performance of dynamical codes is more complicated than for static codes because error detection depends on when an error occurs within the measurement schedule. In this work, we introduce a mapping from the measurement sequence of a Floquet code to a static spacetime subsystem code and show that calculating the distance of a Floquet code can be reduced to calculating the distance of the corresponding static subsystem code. Crucially, our mapping preserves code distance, a property that is not guaranteed for general spacetime code mappings. This reduction converts the dynamical distance problem into a static subsystem code problem, substantially simplifying the analysis of Floquet measurement schedules and facilitating the evaluation of fault tolerance for new measurement schemes.

item.title: Experimental Quantum Hardware Benchmarks of Flat Non-Clifford Hypergraph States, Antipodal Obstructions, and Nonlocal Games on IBM Heron r2
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Realized non-Clifford hypergraph states and contextuality games on Heron r2 QPUs, attaining a 3-qubit CCZ rotated Mermin-3 win rate of 83.95±0.29% (classical bound 75.00%) and beating the classical GHZ bound up to n=30 qubits (59.46±0.54% vs. 50.00%). Calibration-aware layout reaches a 96.85±0.09% raw win rate on the Mermin–Peres magic square.

Grade 0.421 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Filipe Martins Vono, Valéria Gonzaga Santos, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo

Figure

Win rates and margins across benchmarks on ibm_fez. Panels show Mermin-Peres magic square progression compared to Willow, GHZ parity game win rates versus classical ceilings up to 50 qubits, and non-Clifford CCZ and degree-3/4 parity witness advantages.

Asks

Can quantum nonlocal games and contextuality benchmarks be pushed past the Clifford-stabilizer regime to non-Clifford hypergraph states on superconducting processors?

Before

For Mermin-Peres magic square on superconducting processors, Google Willow achieved 98.30% raw win rate (Science 2026). Prior Clifford contextuality benchmarks were restricted to quadratic phase polynomials (deg⁡f≤2).

But

Single-chip benchmarks do not close relativistic locality loopholes. Finite-sample limits saturate direct X-basis total variation distance at 4,096 shots for n=16, and a coherence cliff occurs at Heavy-Hex depth 513 (0.00% return probability).

Tools

IBM Heron r2 processors (ibm_fez, ibm_kingston) · Qiskit Runtime SamplerV2 · Lean 4-verified modular Walsh certifier · Barrier-protected Loschmidt echoes (U_f^† U_f)

Abstract

Real-hardware demonstrations of quantum contextuality have reached high precision on superconducting processors, exemplified by Google Quantum AI's Mermin-Peres magic square and stabilizer games on Willow (Science, 2026). Extending such benchmarks beyond the Clifford regime requires non-Clifford hypergraph states |ψ_f> = 2^-n/2 ∑_x (-1)^f(x) |x> governed by discrete algebraic invariants. Building on our Lean 4-verified framework of Modular Walsh Rigidity and Antipodal Obstructions, we present an experimental study on two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors (ibm_fez, ibm_kingston) across 3 to 50 qubits and 11 auditable jobs (2.13 RUs total). First, we verify antipodal obstructions and mod-17 Walsh rigidity for degree-3/4 states (n=6,8,10), observing 5.4x-11.6x X-basis flatness separation between bent states, obstructed controls, and a degree-4 mod-3 fooler (W = +-1 mod 3), plus n=7 nonlinearity extraction (54.83 vs. 56.00). Second, barrier-protected Loschmidt echoes confirm non-Clifford coherence up to genuinely entangled 16-qubit degree-4 states (1,488x above random on ibm_fez; 17,296x on ibm_kingston for 2x8q, a 2.87x cross-chip gain) and locate a Heavy-Hex depth-513 coherence cliff. Third, calibration-aware layout raises the raw Mermin-Peres win rate on ibm_fez to 96.85 +- 0.09% raw (+87.4 sigma above 88.89% classical; 1.45 pp below Willow's 98.30% raw), while a tensored SPAM diagnostic reaches 98.35%. Uniformly random even-weight GHZ parity games beat the classical bound up to n=30 (89.44% [+79.4 sigma] at 6q to 59.46 +- 0.54% [+17.4 sigma] at 30q). Finally, 3-qubit CCZ rotated Mermin-3 (83.95 +- 0.29%, +31.2 sigma) and Hardy/Guhne-Cabello (77.15 +- 0.33%, +6.5 sigma) games strictly violate the exhaustive 75.00% LHV ceiling, and degree-3/4 antipodal parity witnesses achieve up to +45.87 pp (n=12) and +35.79 pp joint advantage on connected 16-qubit degree-4 states.
